# Proteins without a microscope

Look up `P38398` in AlphaFold DB and you get a picture: one chain, folded,
turning on the screen, colored along its length. The accession is human BRCA1,
the protein Chapter 5 ended up at. Thirty-three experimental structures of it
exist, and every one of them covers a piece of the chain. Nobody has ever seen
the shape of the whole thing. So what is that picture of?

## The protein has its own database

Chapter 5 ended at `NP_009225.1`, NCBI's protein record for BRCA1, 1,863 amino
acids long. It's a sequence with a few notes attached. UniProt holds the same
protein the other way round: one entry per protein, with the sequence
underneath and the annotation piled on top.

What gets piled on is what the protein does, which residues do it, and which
structures exist. The human BRCA1 entry is `P38398`. Open `uniprot.org` and
search for that accession, because the rest of this chapter reads off it. Here
are the values it uses, written out.

``` {.default .output}
Accession   P38398
Entry name  BRCA1_HUMAN
Status      UniProtKB reviewed (Swiss-Prot)
Name        Breast cancer type 1 susceptibility protein
Length      1863 amino acids
Mass        207721 Da
Structures  33 PDB entries
```

Two databases, two accessions, one number. `NP_009225.1` and `P38398` both say
1,863 amino acids. That match is your check that you're on the right record,
and it isn't more than that. Both curators worked from the same submitted
sequences, so the agreement isn't two independent measurements landing in the
same place. If the two lengths ever disagree, one of them is describing a
different form of the protein and you need to find out which.

The mass is 207,721 daltons, and a dalton is roughly the mass of one hydrogen
atom. Nobody weighed anything to get it. UniProt's own documentation says the
mass is calculated from the amino acid composition of the sequence. It leaves
out everything a cell bolts onto a protein after it's made. So the number is
exact about the sequence and silent about the molecule.

::: {.asof}
Checked against the live UniProt interface on 2 August 2026. The accession
`P38398` is the stable handle and it won't move. The entry name `BRCA1_HUMAN`
is the readable one, and readable names do get changed. Cite the accession.
:::

### Reviewed and unreviewed, which you have already met

UniProt comes in two halves, and the half an entry sits in is printed on it.
Reviewed (Swiss-Prot) means a curator read the papers and the sequence and put
their name behind the entry. Unreviewed (TrEMBL) means software translated a
coding sequence, filed the result, and nobody looked at it.

You've seen this split before, wearing different clothes. In Chapter 5, `NM_`
meant a curated transcript and `XM_` meant one predicted by software from a
genome annotation. Same distinction, same consequence: both halves are worth
having, and only one of them is evidence that a person checked.

`P38398` is reviewed. For a human gene this heavily studied, that's what you
should expect, and a search that hands you an unreviewed entry for BRCA1 has
handed you the wrong record.

### A domain is a part that folds by itself

Cut a stretch out of the middle of a protein, make just that stretch in a tube,
and usually you get a tangle. Some stretches fold up anyway, into the same
shape they hold inside the full protein, and go on doing the same job. A
stretch that behaves like that is a [domain]{.term def="A stretch of a protein
that folds up on its own and does its own job. Domains are annotated by the
residue numbers they run between."}, and that's why domains get names and
residue ranges of their own.

The BRCA1 entry annotates three of them. The numbers are positions along the
chain, and the first amino acid is number 1.

``` {.default .output}
Zinc finger   24-65        RING-type
Domain        1642-1736    BRCT 1
Domain        1756-1855    BRCT 2
```

UniProt files the first one under a different heading, Zinc finger, because
that's the kind of thing it is. It folds on its own like the other two, so this
chapter counts it.

Read the positions and you can see how thin the annotation is. One domain sits
inside the first 65 residues. The other two sit at the far end, starting at
residue 1,642. Everything between them is annotated as something else, or as
nothing at all.

Residue numbers are how a claim about a protein gets attached to a place. A
paper reporting a change at residue 1,700 is reporting a change inside BRCT 1,
and you can read that off the block above without knowing any structural
biology. Without the numbers you'd have a change in "the protein", which is
1,863 residues wide and no help to anybody.

## Thirty-three structures of a 1,863-residue protein

The entry lists 33 PDB structures. That sounds like a well-covered protein. Do
the arithmetic before you believe it.

BRCT 1 runs from residue 1,642 to residue 1,736. The number of residues is
1,736 − 1,642 + 1 = 95, and the plus one is there because the range includes
both ends. BRCT 2 runs 1,756 to 1,855, so 1,855 − 1,756 + 1 = 100 residues.

Take the two together with the short linker between them and you get one
continuous block, from 1,642 to 1,855: 1,855 − 1,642 + 1 = 214 residues.

Now divide. 214 / 1863 = 0.115, so the BRCT block is about 11 percent of the
protein. Throw in the RING-type zinc finger, which is 65 − 24 + 1 = 42
residues, and the annotated domains come to 214 + 42 = 256. That leaves
1,863 − 256 = 1,607 residues of BRCA1 outside any annotated domain.

::: {.check}
Do 1,855 − 1,642 + 1 on paper before reading on. If you got 213, you dropped
the plus one and you're counting fenceposts. That's the same off-by-one as
Chapter 5. It's the most expensive arithmetic error in this field, and
Chapter 11 spends a long section on it.
:::

<!-- nlr-allow: 1607 1700 213 1.54 -->

So 33 experimental structures exist, and they cluster on the two ends of the
chain where the domains are. The middle of BRCA1 has never been crystallized.
Not one of the 33 holds a single atom from it.

Here's why that isn't a gap somebody forgot to fill. X-ray crystallography
needs a crystal, and a crystal is millions of copies of the same molecule
stacked in the same orientation in a regular lattice. A domain that folds on
its own is a good candidate for one. Each copy has the same shape, so the
copies stack. A stretch of chain that doesn't settle into one shape has
nothing to stack, and you get no crystal, or a crystal that tells you almost
nothing.

Structural biology therefore reports on the parts of a protein that hold still.
The method has that limit built into it, and the limit shows up in every
structure count you'll ever read. A protein with 33 structures isn't 33 times
better understood than a protein with one. It might be one small domain that
behaves in a tube, solved over and over with different partners bound to it.

Here's the same count on a protein that does hold still. Hemoglobin
subunit beta is `P68871`, it's 147 amino acids long, and UniProt lists 340 PDB
structures for it. That's less than a twelfth of BRCA1's length carrying more
than ten times the structures. The count tracks how well a protein behaves in a
tube, not how important it is or how hard anyone has worked on it.

::: {.why}
A sequence tells you which residues sit next to each other along the chain. A
structure tells you which ones sit next to each other in space, and those are
two different lists. Fold the chain up and two residues 200 apart in the
sequence can end up touching. The pocket that grips a partner molecule is built
out of residues collected from all over the protein. You can't find it by
reading the sequence, however hard you stare. A structure is what turns "this
change is at residue 1,700" into "this change is in the part that does the
gripping".
:::

## Two structures of the same domains

Look `1JNX` up on `rcsb.org` to see what one experiment actually delivered.
It's called "Crystal structure of the BRCT repeat region from the breast
cancer associated protein, BRCA1". It was determined by X-ray diffraction, to
2.5 angstroms, and deposited on 26 July 2001. It covers the BRCT block you just
measured, at the far end of the chain, and nothing else.

`1T15` is called "Crystal Structure of the Brca1 BRCT Domains in Complex with
the Phosphorylated Interacting Region from Bach1 Helicase". Also X-ray, also
the BRCT domains, deposited on 15 April 2004, at 1.85 angstroms. The words
after "in Complex with" matter: this structure has a second molecule in it, a
short piece of another protein caught in the act of being held.

::: {.asof}
Checked against the live RCSB PDB interface on 2 August 2026. Every PDB entry
carries an identifier like `1JNX`, a title, an experimental method, and a
deposition date under some name, however the page is laid out. Those four are
what this chapter uses.
:::

### Resolution, and why 1.85 beats 2.5

An angstrom is a tenth of a nanometer, and a single bond between two carbon
atoms is about 1.54 angstroms long. Hold on to that, because it makes the next
number readable.

Resolution is the size of the smallest detail the experiment can separate.
Features closer together than that blur into one lump. At 2.5 angstroms you can
see the path of the chain and the general bulk of the side chains. You can't
see two bonded carbon atoms as two things, because they sit 1.54 angstroms
apart and the experiment can't split anything closer than 2.5. At 1.85
angstroms the map is sharper and more of the final model is pinned down by the
data.

Smaller is better here, which reads backwards until you remember what the
number measures. Resolution is a blur width. A wider blur is less detail.

::: {.trap}
Every atom in a structure file carries three coordinates, printed to three
decimal places. That's a thousandth of an angstrom, in a structure whose blur
width is 2.5 angstroms. Read the decimals as precision and you'll trust a
position a couple of thousand times further than the experiment can support.
The coordinates are a model somebody fitted into a blurry map, and the file
format has no way to print how blurry.
:::

## The picture on the AlphaFold page

Now the entry this chapter opened on. Open `alphafold.ebi.ac.uk`, search for
`P38398`, and keep the page in front of you for the rest of this section.
AlphaFold DB holds a predicted structure for that accession under the
identifier `AF-P38398-F1`. The one on the page as this was written is model
version 6, created on 1 August 2025, and it covers all 1,863 residues.

All 1,863, including the 1,607 residues outside every annotated domain and the
whole middle of the chain, where no experiment has ever placed an atom. Those
residues get three coordinates printed to three decimal places, exactly like
the residues an experiment did place. Telling the two apart is the rest of this
chapter, and the model will help you do it.

AlphaFold predicts a structure from the sequence. It was trained on the
structures that experiments did produce, so it has seen a great many folded
domains and learned what they look like. For a domain that resembles things in
its training data, the prediction can be close to what an experiment finds. For
a region unlike anything that ever crystallized, the model still hands back a
full set of coordinates. It has no way to hand back nothing.

### pLDDT is the model marking its own work

Every residue in an AlphaFold model carries a
[pLDDT]{.term def="AlphaFold's per-residue confidence in its own prediction, from
0 to 100. High means the model is sure of the local shape. It is not a
measurement."} score from 0 to 100. It's the model's confidence in its own
answer for that residue, and it comes out of the same network that produced the
coordinates. No experiment enters into it. Nothing checked it.

AlphaFold DB's own documentation cuts that range into four named bands, and the
same four turn up wherever this output does. Above 90 is very high. Between 70
and 90 is confident. Between 50 and 70 is low. Below 50 is very low. The
picture is colored by those bands, so a glance tells you where the model is
sure and where it isn't.

Here's the part people get wrong. A long stretch of low pLDDT usually isn't the
prediction failing. It's the model saying that this stretch has no single fixed
shape, and for many proteins that's the correct answer. UniProt annotates
several regions of BRCA1 as disordered, one of them running from residue 230 to
residue 270. Disordered means what it sounds like: in a real cell that piece
moves, and it never settles into one arrangement long enough for anybody to
call it a structure.

So a low-confidence region is a drawing of an answer the model declined to
give. Read the confidence first and the shape second.

::: {.trap}
Take two residues in a low-confidence stretch, measure the distance between
them in the model, and write it in your notes. Nothing errors. Every tool that
reads structures will compute that distance and print it to three decimals,
because the file has coordinates for every atom in the chain. The number is
meaningless, and no software will say so. Check the confidence band before you
measure anything.
:::

Both of those traps come down to reading the confidence before the shape, so
you need to know where AlphaFold DB puts the confidence.

::: {.asof}
Checked against the live AlphaFold DB interface on 2 August 2026. Models get
recomputed and the version number rises, so the one on your screen may be later
than the one printed here. Three things are on that entry under some name: the
model colored by confidence, a key saying which color means which band, and a
per-residue confidence plot along the chain. Find those and the layout doesn't
matter.
:::

## Exercises

::: {.exercise num="8.1" time="30 minutes"}
::: {.goal}
Find the predicted structure for `P38398` and locate one named domain in it by
residue number.
:::
::: {.given}
The three annotated domains and their residue ranges are in the block earlier
in this chapter. Pick any one of them.
:::
::: {.produce}
Three values: the AlphaFold entry identifier, the residue range of the domain
you chose, and the confidence band the model reports across that range, named
as one of very high, confident, low or very low.
:::
::: {.check}
Write your prediction down before you look. A domain folds on its own, and all
three of these have been solved experimentally, which makes them the easiest
cases a predictor ever gets. Expect one of the two top bands. If you land in
low or very low over an annotated domain, check that you're counting residues
from the start of the chain.
:::

::: {.answerspace lines="5"}
:::
:::

::: {.exercise num="8.2" time="35 minutes"}
::: {.goal}
Put the AlphaFold model of BRCA1 next to `1JNX` and say what the experiment
covers that the model doesn't, and the other way round.
:::
::: {.given}
`1JNX` is the BRCT repeat region at 2.5 angstroms. The AlphaFold model covers
1,863 residues. The BRCT block runs from residue 1,642 to residue 1,855.
:::
::: {.produce}
Four things: the number of residues in the BRCT block, that number as a
fraction of the whole protein, one sentence on what `1JNX` can tell you that
the model can't, and one sentence on what the model shows you that `1JNX`
doesn't.
:::
::: {.check}
Your fraction should be about 11 percent. You can get there from two numbers in
this chapter: subtract, add one, divide. If you wrote something near 100
percent, you used the length of the model instead of the length of the
experimental structure. That mistake is the whole reason this exercise exists.
:::

::: {.answerspace lines="6"}
:::
:::

## If it breaks

::: {.ifbreaks}
::: {.errfix err="Searching BRCA1 in UniProt returns dozens of entries"}
The search covers every species and both halves of the database at once. Narrow
it to human and to reviewed entries, or go straight to the accession `P38398`,
which is one record and can't be ambiguous.
:::

::: {.errfix err="The AlphaFold model version is higher than 6"}
The model was recomputed after this page was written, which is the system
working as intended. Use what's on the page and write down the version you
used, the same way you wrote down the dot in `NM_007294.4` in Chapter 5.
:::

::: {.errfix err="Residue numbers in the PDB entry do not match the UniProt ones"}
A PDB entry holds a fragment, and the numbering inside it doesn't have to start
at 1 or to match UniProt. The entry carries a mapping back to `P38398`. Find
that mapping and convert before you compare anything, because an unconverted
residue number will look perfectly reasonable and point at the wrong place.
:::

::: {.errfix err="The structure viewer stays blank or never finishes loading"}
That's the network or the browser, not the database. A viewer downloads the
coordinates and then renders them in 3D, which some machines and some
connections won't do. Neither exercise needs the picture to turn: the
identifier, the residue range and the confidence band all come off the text and
the confidence plot on the same page.
:::
:::

::: {.checkpoint}
- Read a UniProt entry and say whether it's reviewed or unreviewed, and what
  that tells you about who checked it
- Name the three annotated domains of BRCA1 and give the residue range of each
- Convert a residue range into a count of residues, and into a fraction of the
  whole protein
- Explain why 33 experimental structures do not cover 33 parts of a protein
- Say what a resolution of 2.5 angstroms lets you see and what it doesn't
- Distinguish a pLDDT score from a measurement, and say what a long low-pLDDT
  stretch usually means
:::
